## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Sources disagree about the best tide.
- Limited information is available about the wave sizes this break works in.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.
- No survey, scientific or official source confirms the best wind direction.

| Variable | Research confidence | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Swell direction | High | Supported by 6 independent sources, including a forecast site's spot guide. |
| Swell size | Low | Supported by one source (a community source). |
| Swell period | Low | No sources found. |
| Wind | Moderate | Supported by 2 independent sources, including a forecast site's spot guide. |
| Tide | Low | Supported by 2 independent sources, including a surf magazine; 1 disagrees. |
| Bottom / bathymetry | High | Described by 7 independent sources, including survey data. |
| Season | High | Supported by 4 independent sources, including a forecast site's spot guide. |
| How the wave breaks | High | Described by 6 independent sources, including a published surf guide. |

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Re-read 4 of 7 current sources (surf-forecast.com, WannaSurf and two WSL posts). surfertoday.com and surfer.com returned 403. The Stormrider break page returns 200, but its guide text is only in a JavaScript data payload, so it cannot be verified with check_excerpt. That payload reads: 'An often stellar cobblestone peak, Lowers provides occasional hollow, zippering lefts, but is more known for its long, fast, bowling rights. Best with SW swells up to double-overhead. Can be good at any tide.' It is kept as web_search, unchanged. New readable sources: Stab (2016, Tanner Gudauskas) and Pacific Surf School's blog (2025, community). Wind: surf-forecast.com (NE = 45 deg, matches the profile) is the only readable source giving an offshore direction. WannaSurf lists an SE/E/NE wind window, WSL/Biolos says any light wind except south, and Pacific Surf mentions morning offshores, all with value null. Tide conflict: WannaSurf (mid) and WSL/Biolos (mid to incoming) support the profile's mid, but surf-forecast.com says tide does not affect quality. Stormrider (unverifiable payload) also says any tide. Size: WSL gives a head-high to overhead sweet spot (about 5-8 ft) and says it handles virtually any size. WannaSurf says it holds 12 ft+, above the profile's 10 ft maximum, and Stormrider's payload says 'up to double-overhead' (roughly 10-12 ft faces), so the 10 ft maximum looks conservative. Direction: the profile's 180-215 optimum is supported by WSL/Biolos (S) and surf-forecast.com and Pacific Surf (SW 225, 10 deg outside the optimum). Biolos warns that SE hurricane swells are bad, which questions the 150 deg end of the window. Season: surf-forecast.com (summer) and Pacific Surf (April-October) fit the May-October profile. Swell period: still no number from any readable source; WSL's 'long' period is Surfline's. Classification: WSL editorial pages are now 'magazine' per methodology v1.2 (previously 'official').

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives southwest as the ideal swell direction and Pacific Surf School says especially southwest swells, while Matt Biolos (WSL 2016) says the best direction is definitely south and SURFER (search summary) that south swells wrap in; SurferToday (search summary) says S/SW.

  - S5 (Pacific Surf School): “allows Trestles to pick up a wide range of swell directions, especially southwest swells”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “The best swell direction is definitely a South,”
  - S8 (SURFER Magazine): “if there's a whiff of a south swell, it will wrap into the joint”
  - S6 (SurferToday): “A large S/SW swell and light-to-moderate E/NE winds are the ideal setup.”
- **Acceptable range**: WannaSurf lists north, northwest, west, southwest and south as good (the evidence file questions the N and NW entries), Pacific Surf School says it picks up a wide range of swell directions, and Tanner Gudauskas (Stab 2016) that the left takes a little more west and south.
  - S2 (WannaSurf): “Good swell directionNorth, NorthWest, West, SouthWest, South”
  - S5 (Pacific Surf School): “allows Trestles to pick up a wide range of swell directions, especially southwest swells”
  - S4 (Stab Magazine): “I think the left is more versatile at Lowers. It takes a little more west and south, which is ultimate summertime conditions.”
- **Blocked directions**: No excerpt names swell directions that are blocked or shadowed by land or reefs.
- **Exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach and reef break with very reliable surf, and Pacific Surf School says it picks up a wide range of swell directions.
  - S1 (Surf-Forecast.com): “is an exposed beach and reef break that has very reliable surf”
  - S5 (Pacific Surf School): “allows Trestles to pick up a wide range of swell directions, especially southwest swells”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell direction · ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast gives southwest as the ideal swell direction and Pacific Surf School says especially southwest swells, while Matt Biolos (WSL 2016) says the best direction is definitely south and SURFER (search summary) that south swells wrap in; SurferToday (search summary) says S/SW.
- **Tide · preferred stage**: WannaSurf gives mid tide as best and Matt Biolos (WSL 2016) a mid to incoming tide for Southern Hemisphere swell, while Surf-Forecast says surf quality isn't affected by the tide; Biolos adds that the cobblestone bottom keeps waves clean on most tides.
- **Geography · break type**: WannaSurf calls it a right-and-left point break and Pacific Surf School a cobblestone reef forming a point break, Stormrider (search summary) a cobblestone peak and SurferToday (search summary) an A-frame, while Surf-Forecast calls it an exposed beach and reef break with a left and a better right.
